c: A coil with a memory

Any current creates a magnetic field around its wire. Wind the wire into a coil and the fields of the turns add together. Building that field takes energy, and collapsing it gives the energy back. The result is a part that resists changes in current the way a heavy flywheel resists changes in speed. Its strength is called inductance, measured in henries, with real parts usually in microhenries or millihenries. Adding an iron or ferrite core concentrates the field and multiplies the inductance many times over.
The mirror image of a capacitor

A capacitor resists changes in voltage and passes fast signals easily. An inductor resists changes in current and passes steady current easily while opposing fast changes. Put simply, capacitors block DC and inductors block high frequencies. Used together they make filters that select or reject a band of frequencies. An old radio tuning dial moved the plates of a capacitor against a fixed coil to choose a station. The same pairing is still inside every radio, phone and wireless charger made today.
Kickback

Because an inductor insists that its current keep flowing, interrupting that current abruptly has a dramatic effect. The collapsing field generates whatever voltage it needs to keep the current going, often hundreds of volts from a 12 volt circuit. This is how a car's ignition coil makes a spark. It is also how a relay or motor destroys the transistor that switches it. The cure is a diode placed backwards across the coil, called a flyback diode, which gives the current a harmless loop to die away in.
How switching supplies use it

The inductor's stubbornness is what makes efficient power conversion possible. A switching regulator connects an inductor to the supply for a moment, storing energy in its field, then disconnects it and lets the inductor deliver that energy to the output. Doing this hundreds of thousands of times a second, and varying how long the switch stays on, produces a lower or higher voltage with very little wasted as heat. Phone chargers, laptop adapters and the converters on every motherboard work this way.
Transformers are two inductors sharing a field

Wind two coils on the same core and a changing current in the first induces a voltage in the second. The ratio of the turns sets the ratio of the voltages. Ten times the turns on the output gives ten times the voltage and a tenth of the current. Because only a changing field induces anything, transformers work on AC and not on steady DC. They also isolate: no wire connects the input to the output, which is what makes a mains adapter safe to touch on its low voltage side.
Ferrite beads and chokes

An inductor used simply to block unwanted high frequency noise is called a choke. The lump moulded onto many laptop and monitor cables is a ferrite sleeve doing this job, soaking up radio frequency interference travelling along the wire. On circuit boards, tiny ferrite beads sit in series with power lines to keep the noise of one section out of another. They cost almost nothing and are often the difference between a product that passes its radio emissions test and one that fails it.
Reading an inductor's limits

Two ratings matter beyond the inductance. The saturation current is the point at which the core cannot hold any more magnetic field. Past it the inductance collapses and the current shoots up, a common cause of failed power converters. The resistance of the winding is the other, since it wastes power as heat. A physically larger inductor of the same value generally has a higher saturation current and lower resistance. When a design calls for a specific inductor, substitute by all three numbers, never by inductance alone.
What seasoning is

The dark surface on a cast iron pan is not a coating applied at the factory in the usual sense, and it is not a layer of old grease. It is oil that has been heated until it changed chemically, linking into a hard, plastic-like film bonded to the metal. This process is called polymerization. A well-built layer protects the iron from rust and gives a surface that releases food easily, though it is never quite as slippery as a modern non-stick coating.
How to build it

To season a pan, rub it all over with a very thin film of cooking oil, then wipe off as much as you can, as if you had made a mistake. Bake it upside down in a hot oven, around 230 degrees Celsius or 450 Fahrenheit, for an hour, and let it cool. Repeating this a few times builds a durable base. Thick layers of oil turn sticky and flake. Thin ones cure hard. After that, ordinary cooking with fat adds to it.
Soap is fine

The best-known rule is never to use soap. It dates from when soap contained lye, which does attack seasoning. Modern washing-up liquid is a mild detergent and will not harm a properly cured surface, because polymerized oil is no longer oil. Wash the pan with a little soap and a brush or sponge. What you should avoid is leaving it to soak or putting it in the dishwasher, both of which promote rust.
Dry it and oil it

Water is the real enemy. After washing, dry the pan at once with a towel, then set it over a low flame for a minute to drive off the last moisture. While it is still warm, wipe on a few drops of oil and rub until the surface looks dry. This takes under two minutes and is the whole of routine maintenance. A pan treated this way improves with every use.
How it handles heat

Cast iron is often said to heat evenly. It does not. Iron conducts heat more slowly than aluminium or copper, so a pan placed on a burner develops a hot spot over the flame. What it does well is hold heat, because it is thick and heavy. Once fully hot, it stays hot when cold food is added, which is why it sears so well. The answer is patience: preheat it over moderate heat for five to ten minutes.
What to cook, and what to wait on

A new pan's seasoning is thin. Start with foods that are forgiving and add fat: bacon, sausages, shallow-fried potatoes, cornbread, seared meat. Hold off on delicate eggs and fish until the surface has built up. Long simmering of acidic foods, such as tomato sauce or wine, can wear thin seasoning and leave a metallic taste. A quick acidic pan sauce does no harm. Once the pan is well seasoned, it tolerates nearly anything.
Rust and rescue

A rusty or neglected pan is not ruined. Scrub the rust away with steel wool or coarse salt, wash, dry thoroughly and season it again from scratch. Pans found at flea markets in dreadful condition are regularly restored this way, and many cooks prefer older ones for their smoother cooking surface. Short of cracking it or warping it by plunging it hot into cold water, there is very little you can do to cast iron that cannot be undone.
Is it worth it

Cast iron is cheap, nearly indestructible and moves from hob to oven to campfire. It gives a crust on meat and cornbread that thin pans cannot match. Its drawbacks are weight and slowness to heat. It is not the best tool for everything. For quick sauces or boiling, lighter pans respond faster. As one pan among several, used for searing, roasting and baking, it earns its space for decades.
The coin flip nobody takes

Suppose you are offered a bet on a fair coin. Heads you win 150 dollars, tails you lose 100. On average the bet is clearly in your favour. Most people refuse it. Asked how much the win would need to be before they accepted, the typical answer is around 200 dollars, twice the possible loss. This finding is central to prospect theory, the account of decisions under risk that Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published in 1979.
Gains and losses, not wealth

Older economic theory assumed people judge outcomes by their final level of wealth. Prospect theory showed that people instead judge changes relative to a reference point, usually where they are now. A gain and a loss of the same size are not mirror images. The loss weighs roughly twice as much. Later critics have argued that the effect is weaker or absent for small stakes, and the exact ratio is debated. For decisions that matter, the asymmetry shows up reliably.
The endowment effect

One consequence is that people value things more once they own them. In a classic experiment, half of a group of students were given a university mug and then allowed to trade. Economic theory predicted that about half the mugs would change hands. Very few did. Owners demanded about twice as much to give up a mug as the others were willing to pay for one. Giving up the mug registered as a loss, and losses are expensive.
Holding losers, selling winners

Investors show the pattern clearly. Studies of brokerage accounts have found that people are considerably more likely to sell a share that has risen than one that has fallen. Selling a loser turns a paper loss into a real one, which is painful, so they wait to get back to even. The market has no memory of what they paid. The result is often that winners are sold too soon and losers are kept too long, the reverse of what would serve them.
Framing

Because reactions depend on whether something is seen as a gain or a loss, the same facts produce different choices depending on how they are described. A surgery with a 90 percent survival rate is chosen more often than one with a 10 percent mortality rate. A discount for paying cash is accepted where a surcharge for using a card causes resentment. The outcomes are identical. Only the reference point implied by the wording has moved.
The status quo

Loss aversion also explains a general reluctance to change. Any change involves giving up some things to gain others, and the things given up loom larger. So people stay with their default pension fund, their current supplier and their existing job longer than a neutral calculation would suggest. Organizations that understand this set helpful defaults, such as enrolling staff in a savings plan automatically and letting them opt out, which raises participation dramatically.
When it protects you

The instinct is not simply an error. For most of human history, a serious loss could mean starvation, while an equivalent gain meant only a better week. Caution about losses kept people alive. It still protects against ruinous bets. The trouble arises when the instinct fires over small, repeated risks where the odds favour you. Refusing every such bet means giving up a great deal over a lifetime in exchange for avoiding minor disappointments.
Working around it

A few questions help. Would I buy this today at the current price if I did not already own it? If not, why am I keeping it? Am I judging this choice on its own, or as one of many similar choices I will make over the years, where the averages will work in my favour? And what exactly is my reference point, and is it still the right one? Naming the feeling as loss aversion often loosens its hold.
The misunderstanding

Many people believe that if a raise moves them into a higher tax bracket, all of their income is then taxed at the higher rate. Some have turned down overtime because of it. In a marginal tax system, which is what the United States and most other countries use for income tax, this is simply wrong. The higher rate applies only to the dollars above the threshold. Everything below it is taxed exactly as before.
Buckets, not a single rate

Picture your income filling a row of buckets, one after another. The first bucket is taxed at the lowest rate. When it is full, income spills into the second, taxed at the next rate, and so on. Take an invented system to keep the numbers simple: 10 percent on the first 10,000 dollars, 20 percent on the next 30,000, and 30 percent on everything above 40,000. Each rate touches only the money inside its own bucket.
A worked example

Someone earning 50,000 dollars under that invented system pays 10 percent of the first 10,000, which is 1,000. Then 20 percent of the next 30,000, which is 6,000. Then 30 percent of the final 10,000, which is 3,000. The total is 10,000 dollars. This person is in the 30 percent bracket, yet their tax is 20 percent of their income. Being in a bracket describes only the rate on your last dollars.
Marginal and effective

Two rates describe every taxpayer. The marginal rate is the rate on the next dollar you earn, 30 percent in the example. The effective rate is total tax divided by total income, 20 percent in the example. They answer different questions. Use the marginal rate to judge a decision at the edge: the value of a deduction, or what you keep from overtime. Use the effective rate to understand what share of your income actually goes to tax.
What happens with a raise

Suppose the same person gets a raise of 5,000 dollars. All of it lands in the top bucket and is taxed at 30 percent, so they pay 1,500 more in tax and keep 3,500. Their take-home pay has gone up. No amount of extra income, under a purely marginal system, can reduce what you keep. Had they been just below the 40,000 threshold, the dollars above it would be taxed at 30 percent and the dollars below would be untouched.
Deductions and credits

The same logic explains two terms people often confuse. A deduction reduces the income that is taxed, so it saves you its amount multiplied by your marginal rate. A 1,000 dollar deduction is worth 300 dollars to someone in a 30 percent bracket and 100 dollars to someone in a 10 percent bracket. A credit reduces the tax itself, dollar for dollar. A 1,000 dollar credit is worth 1,000 dollars to everyone who owes at least that much.
The real exceptions

There are cases where earning more does leave someone worse off, but they come from outside the bracket system. Certain benefits and subsidies are withdrawn once income passes a set level, sometimes all at once. A person just over such a line can lose more in support than they gained in pay. These are called benefit cliffs, and they are a genuine problem for households near them. The cause is the design of those programmes, not the tax brackets.
Why this matters

Understanding marginal rates changes practical decisions. You should not refuse a raise, a bonus or extra hours on tax grounds. Contributions to tax-deferred retirement accounts are most valuable when your marginal rate is high. And when you hear a proposal to raise the top rate, you can work out what it means: it changes the tax on income above the top threshold only. Real brackets and thresholds change from year to year, so check the current figures for your own country.
Who acts when

Hold'em is played in a circle, and a small disc called the button marks the nominal dealer. After the flop, the player on the button acts last on every round of betting. The two players to the button's left post the forced bets, the small blind and the big blind, and must act first after the flop. Everyone else sits somewhere between. Seats that act early are called early position, and the seats just before the button are late position, the cutoff and the hijack.
Information is the advantage

Acting last means you see what everyone else does before you decide. If they check, they have told you something. If they bet, you know the price before you commit. The player acting first has to decide blind to all of that. Over a single hand the difference is modest. Over thousands of hands it is enormous. Tracking databases from online poker show the same pattern for nearly every player: the button is their most profitable seat and the blinds are where they lose.
Control over the pot

Position also gives you control of the size of the pot. With a strong hand, you can bet when checked to and build it. With a medium hand, you can check behind and take a free card or a cheap showdown. With a draw, you decide whether to pay or to see the next card for nothing. Out of position you have none of these choices. If you check, your opponent decides. If you bet, you may be raised and forced into a guess.
Tight early, wide late

The practical result is that the hands worth playing change with your seat. In early position at a full table, with many players left to act behind you, a sound opening range is narrow, on the order of one hand in seven or eight. On the button, with only the blinds left to act, good players open something like four hands in ten. King nine suited is a clear fold under the gun and a routine raise on the button. The cards are identical. The seat changed their value.
Why the blinds lose

The blinds are a double handicap. You have put money in without seeing your cards, and you will be out of position for the rest of the hand. Even the best players in the world lose money from the blinds over time. The goal there is not to win but to lose less than the full blind you were forced to post. Defending too many weak hands from the blinds, on the theory that you already have chips invested, is a classic and costly habit.
Stealing

Because the button and cutoff act late, they often face a pot in which everyone has folded and only the blinds remain. Raising there with a wide range, called stealing the blinds, wins the pot outright a good share of the time. When it does not, the stealer still gets to play the hand in position. A player who folds the button too often is passing up the best seat at the table, and one who never defends the blinds is giving the stealer free money.
The simple rule

If you remember one thing about position, make it this: play more hands when you will act last and fewer when you will act first. When in doubt about a marginal hand, let your seat break the tie. Many players improve noticeably just by folding the weakest third of the hands they used to play from early position and adding that many on the button. No new skill is required. They are simply playing more of their pots with the advantage.
Waves through two gaps

Around 1801, the English scientist Thomas Young passed light through two narrow slits and let it fall on a screen. He did not see two bright bands. He saw a row of many bright and dark stripes. This is what waves do. Where the crests from one slit meet crests from the other, they reinforce. Where crests meet troughs, they cancel. Water ripples passing through two gaps in a barrier produce the same pattern. Young's result persuaded physicists that light is a wave.
Then light turned out to be lumpy

A century later, the picture grew complicated. Experiments showed that light also arrives in discrete packets of energy, later called photons, and that a detector registers each one as a single click at a single spot. Einstein's explanation of this in 1905 earned him his Nobel Prize. Light seemed to be a wave when travelling and a particle when detected. Then physicists discovered that electrons, which everyone regarded as particles, could produce interference patterns as well.
One at a time

The crucial version of the experiment sends particles through the slits singly, with long gaps between them, so that there is never more than one in the apparatus. Each one lands on the screen as a single dot. At first the dots appear random. As thousands accumulate, the striped interference pattern emerges. Experiments with single electrons, performed in the 1970s and 1980s, show this build-up clearly. Each particle somehow contributes to a pattern that requires both slits.
Watching changes it

The obvious question is which slit each particle went through. So experimenters place a detector at the slits to find out. It works: each particle is found at one slit or the other. But the interference pattern disappears, and the screen shows two plain bands, as if the particles were tiny bullets. Remove the detector and the stripes return. Obtaining the path information, by any means that could in principle reveal it, destroys the interference.
It is not clumsiness

It is tempting to suppose the detector simply knocks the particle off course. The effect runs deeper than that. Experiments have been designed in which the which-path information is recorded very gently, or recorded and then erased before anyone looks. Interference disappears when the information exists and reappears when it is truly erased. What matters is not the disturbance but whether the path could be known. That is a statement about information, and it is very strange.
What the theory says

Quantum mechanics handles all of this with a mathematical object called the wave function. It spreads out, passes through both slits and interferes with itself. Its size at each point on the screen gives the probability that the particle will be detected there. The theory does not say where a given particle will land, only the odds, and those odds match experiment to extraordinary precision. It predicts the pattern perfectly and declines to describe what the particle is doing in between.
Not just tiny things

The effect has been demonstrated with objects far larger than electrons. In 1999 a team in Vienna obtained interference with molecules made of sixty carbon atoms, shaped like footballs. Later experiments have used molecules containing around two thousand atoms. There is no agreed size at which quantum behaviour stops. In practice, large warm objects interact with their surroundings so constantly that the delicate interference is washed out almost instantly.
What physicists make of it

A century on, physicists agree completely on how to calculate and disagree on what it means. Some hold that the wave function is only a tool for prediction. Some hold that every possible outcome occurs in separate branches of reality. Others propose hidden variables guiding each particle. The experiments cannot yet tell these apart. The double slit remains the cleanest demonstration that the world, at its smallest scale, does not work the way everyday objects suggest.
A check valve for electrons

A diode has two leads, the anode and the cathode. Current flows easily from anode to cathode and hardly at all the other way. On the part, a stripe marks the cathode end. On a schematic, the symbol is an arrow pointing at a bar, and the arrow shows the direction current is allowed to flow. Inside is a junction between two differently treated regions of silicon. The junction is the foundation of nearly all semiconductor devices, and a diode is the simplest thing you can build from one.
The forward drop

A diode is not a perfect valve. It needs a small voltage to open, and it keeps roughly that much for itself while conducting. For an ordinary silicon diode the figure is about 0.6 to 0.7 volts. Below it almost nothing flows. Above it the current rises steeply. That lost voltage becomes heat: a diode carrying 3 amps with 0.7 volts across it dissipates about 2 watts. Schottky diodes use a metal junction instead and drop only 0.2 to 0.4 volts, which is why they appear wherever efficiency matters.
Rectifying AC

The classic job is turning AC into DC. One diode passes only the positive half of the wave. Four diodes arranged in a diamond, called a bridge rectifier, steer both halves so they emerge pointing the same way. Follow that with a capacitor and you have rough DC. Every device that plugs into a wall contains this arrangement somewhere near its input. Bridge rectifiers are sold as single four-legged blocks marked with a wave symbol on two legs and plus and minus on the others.
Protecting against mistakes

A diode in series with a power input stops damage if the battery or adapter is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop. A diode across a relay coil absorbs the voltage spike when the coil is switched off. Two diodes from an input pin to the supply rails clamp any spike to a safe level, and most chips have these built in. Protection is unglamorous, but it is the reason modern gadgets survive static shocks and reversed plugs that would have destroyed electronics of fifty years ago.
Zener diodes work backwards on purpose

Every diode breaks down and conducts if enough reverse voltage is applied. A Zener diode is built so that this happens at a precise, repeatable voltage, such as 5.1 or 12 volts, without harming it. Wired in reverse with a resistor in series, it holds a steady voltage across itself while the input varies. It makes a simple voltage reference or a clamp that keeps a line from rising too high. For precision, a dedicated reference chip is better, but a Zener is cheap and nearly indestructible.
Light in, light out

Some diodes are built to interact with light. An LED emits light when current flows forward through it, with the colour set by the material. A photodiode does the reverse, producing a small current when light falls on it, and is the sensor in remote control receivers, smoke detectors and fibre optic links. A solar cell is a very large photodiode arranged to deliver power. All three are the same junction, optimized for a different job.
Testing a diode

Most multimeters have a diode setting, marked with the diode symbol. It pushes a small current through the part and shows the forward voltage. A good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.7 one way and shows open circuit the other way. A reading near zero both ways means it has failed short. Open both ways means it has failed open. The same test checks the junctions inside a transistor, and with an LED it usually makes the part glow faintly, which conveniently tells you which lead is which.
Why temperature

Harmful bacteria are killed by heat, and the kill depends on reaching a high enough temperature at the centre of the food. You cannot judge that by eye. Chicken can look white while still undercooked, and a burger can turn brown well before it is safe. Cooking times in recipes are estimates that depend on your oven and the thickness of the food. An instant-read digital thermometer costs little and settles the question in seconds.
The four numbers

The United States Department of Agriculture publishes minimum internal temperatures. Poultry, whole or ground, should reach 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 74 Celsius. Ground beef, pork and lamb should reach 160 Fahrenheit, or 71 Celsius. Whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb, such as steaks, chops and roasts, should reach 145 Fahrenheit, or 63 Celsius, and then rest for three minutes. Fish should reach 145 Fahrenheit. Leftovers and casseroles should be reheated to 165.
Why mince is different

A steak can be eaten pink while a burger should be cooked through, and the reason is where the bacteria are. On a whole cut, contamination sits on the surface, which is exposed to the highest heat. The interior is essentially sterile. Grinding mixes the surface throughout the meat, so the centre of a burger may carry the same bacteria as the outside. That is why the safe temperature for ground meat is higher.
Using the thermometer

Insert the probe into the thickest part of the food, away from bone, fat and the pan, all of which give false readings. For a whole bird, check the inner thigh and the thickest part of the breast. For thin foods such as burgers, slide the probe in from the side. Wash the probe between checks. Food continues to rise a few degrees after it leaves the heat, which is part of the reason for resting meat.
The danger zone

Bacteria multiply fastest between about 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, or 4 and 60 Celsius. Food safety agencies call this the danger zone. The rule of thumb is that perishable food should not sit in that range for more than two hours in total, or one hour in hot weather above about 32 Celsius. That includes time on the counter before cooking, on the table after, and in a bag on the way home from the shop.
Cooling and storing

Refrigerators should be at or below 40 Fahrenheit, 4 Celsius, and freezers at 0 Fahrenheit, minus 18 Celsius. Put leftovers away promptly. Large pots of hot food cool slowly in the middle, so divide them into shallow containers first. Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, not on the counter, where the outside warms into the danger zone long before the centre thaws.
Keep raw and cooked apart

Many cases of food poisoning come from cross-contamination, not undercooking. Juices from raw meat reach a salad by way of a chopping board, a knife, a plate or a pair of hands. Use a separate board for raw meat, wash hands with soap after handling it, and never put cooked food back on the plate that held it raw. Food safety agencies also advise against rinsing raw chicken, since splashing spreads bacteria around the sink.
Who needs extra care

Healthy adults usually recover from food poisoning in a few days. Young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems are at much higher risk of serious illness, and for them the guidelines should be followed strictly. When cooking for a group that includes anyone in those categories, use the thermometer and cook to the published temperatures. Severe or prolonged symptoms, or any sign of dehydration, call for medical advice.
A shortcut that usually works

When asked how frequent something is, the mind does not count. It checks how readily instances can be recalled and treats ease as a measure of frequency. Often this works, because common things do tend to be easier to remember. Tversky and Kahneman, who named the shortcut in 1973, called it the availability heuristic. The trouble is that many things besides frequency make an example easy to recall: how recent it was, how dramatic, how emotional, how personal.
The letter K

In one early demonstration, people were asked whether English has more words that begin with the letter K or more words with K as the third letter. Most chose the first. In fact there are more with K in third place. It is simply much easier to search your memory for words by their first letter, so examples such as kitchen and kite arrive quickly, while words such as ask and like have to be dug out. Ease of retrieval was mistaken for abundance.
Risk and the news

The largest distortions involve danger. News reports cover events that are unusual and dramatic, so plane crashes, shark attacks and kidnappings are far more available in memory than their true frequency warrants. Heart disease, falls and car accidents kill vastly more people and generate few headlines. People consistently overestimate deaths from spectacular causes and underestimate those from mundane ones. The result is fear directed at the wrong targets.
A deadly example

After the attacks of September 2001, many Americans avoided flying and drove long distances instead. Driving is much more dangerous per mile than commercial flight. The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer analysed road fatality figures for the following twelve months and estimated that around 1,600 more people died on the roads than would have been expected, a toll several times the number of passengers on the hijacked planes. A vivid fear had steered people toward a greater risk.
Whose effort you remember

Availability also explains a familiar household dispute. When couples are each asked what percentage of the housework they do, the two answers typically add up to well over 100. Each person remembers their own contributions in detail, because they were present for all of them, and recalls the other's only partly. The same happens in teams at work. Nobody is lying. Each is drawing on a sample of memories that over-represents their own efforts.
Recent and personal

One vivid personal experience can outweigh a mountain of statistics. Someone whose neighbour was burgled feels crime is rising whatever the figures say. An investor who lived through a crash stays out of the market for years. A manager who was once let down by a remote worker distrusts remote work. Marketers know that a single story about one customer persuades more people than a table of results from thousands. Stories are available. Numbers are not.
Correcting for it

The remedy is to ask for the count instead of the example. How often does this actually happen, per year, per thousand people? Where would I find that number? Then ask why the example came to mind so easily. Was it on the news, did it happen to someone I know, was it frightening? If the answer is yes, ease of recall is telling you about the storytelling, not about the world. Base your decision on the frequency.
Turning it to good use

The same mechanism can work for you. If you want to remember to do something, make it vivid and visible. If you want people to take a real risk seriously, give them a concrete story alongside the statistics. And if you want an accurate view of your own life, keep a record. People who write down what went well each week are often surprised when they read it back, because memory had kept the frustrations and let most of the rest go.
What the statement is

An income statement, also called a profit and loss statement, reports what a business earned and spent over a period, usually a quarter or a year. It starts with sales and subtracts costs in a fixed order until it arrives at profit. The top line is revenue and the bottom line is net income, which is where the everyday phrases top line and bottom line come from. Reading it is a matter of following the subtraction.
Revenue

Revenue is the total value of goods and services sold in the period. It is recorded when the sale is earned, not necessarily when cash arrives, so a company can report revenue for goods a customer has not yet paid for. Growth in revenue is the first thing analysts look at, but it says nothing about whether the sales were profitable. A business can grow its top line quickly while losing more money on every additional sale.
Cost of goods sold and gross profit

The first subtraction is the direct cost of what was sold: materials, factory labour, or for a retailer the price paid to suppliers. Revenue minus this cost is gross profit. Expressed as a percentage of revenue, it is the gross margin. A software firm may keep 80 cents of each dollar of sales at this stage. A supermarket may keep 25. Gross margin shows how much room a business has to pay for everything else.
Operating expenses

Next come the costs of running the company that are not tied to individual units: salaries of sales and office staff, marketing, rent, research and development. Subtract them from gross profit and you have operating income, the profit from the core business. Many analysts consider it the most informative line, because it leaves out financing and tax, which depend on how the company is funded and where it is based, not on how good the business is.
Below the operating line

After operating income, the statement deducts interest paid on debt and adds any interest earned, then deducts income tax. One-off items also appear here, such as the gain from selling a division or the cost of a lawsuit. What remains is net income. Divide it by the number of shares and you get earnings per share, the figure most quoted in the financial press when a company reports its results.
A tiny example

Imagine a bakery with sales of 500,000 dollars. Flour, butter and bakers' wages cost 200,000, leaving a gross profit of 300,000, a 60 percent gross margin. Rent, counter staff, marketing and equipment wear cost 230,000, leaving operating income of 70,000. Interest on the oven loan takes 10,000 and tax takes 15,000. Net income is 45,000 dollars, a net margin of 9 percent. Nine cents of every dollar a customer hands over ends up as profit.
What to compare

A single statement means little alone. Compare each line with the same period a year earlier to see direction. Compare margins with those of competitors to see relative strength. Look at whether costs are growing faster than revenue. A company whose sales rise 10 percent while its operating expenses rise 20 is heading the wrong way, whatever the headline says. Trends across several years reveal far more than any one period.
What it cannot tell you

The income statement has blind spots. Profit is an accounting figure built on estimates, such as how quickly equipment wears out, and it is not the same as cash. A profitable company can still run out of money. The statement also shows nothing about what the company owns or owes. For those you need its two companions, the cash flow statement and the balance sheet. The three are designed to be read together.
Most hands miss

Start with a sobering fact. Two unpaired cards will make a pair or better on the flop only about one time in three. Two thirds of the time you have nothing but high cards. That is why starting hand selection matters so much. If you enter pots with weak cards, you will usually miss, and when you do hit, you will often hold a second best hand. Folding before the flop is the cheapest decision in the game, and good players do it most of the time.
Big pairs

Aces, kings and queens are the premium hands, strong enough to win unimproved. Their weakness is that they are usually still just one pair after the flop, and one pair loses big pots when the board turns ugly and the money goes in. The standard advice is to raise and reraise them before the flop, building a pot while you are a clear favourite and thinning the field. Slow playing aces against several opponents feels clever and often ends with a small win or a large loss.
Big cards and the kicker problem

Hands such as ace king and ace queen make top pair with a strong second card, called the kicker. That is their job. The danger lies in weaker versions. King jack and ace ten look good but are often dominated, meaning an opponent holds the same high card with a better kicker. When both players make top pair, the dominated hand pays off. Hands like these are where average players lose the most money, because the hand is too good to fold and not good enough to win.
Suited and connected

Being suited adds only a few percentage points to a hand's raw chance of winning. You will flop a flush just under one time in a hundred, and a flush draw about one time in nine. The value of suited connected cards such as 8 7 of hearts lies elsewhere. They make hidden straights and flushes that win big pots, and when they miss, they are easy to fold. They need deep stacks and good position to earn their keep.
Small pairs

Pairs from twos through sixes play one main way. You hope to flop three of a kind, which happens about one time in eight and a half. When it does, the hand is strong and well disguised. When it does not, you usually hold a low pair on a board of higher cards and should let it go. The discipline is the difficult part. A small pair that does not improve is rarely worth more than one cheap look.
Trouble hands

Certain hands have earned the name. Ace with a small unsuited card, king ten offsuit, queen jack offsuit against a raise from early position. They win small pots and lose large ones, because the hands that give them action are the hands that beat them. This does not make them unplayable. On the button, with everyone folded, they are fine raises. Against a raise from a tight player in early position, they are folds, however good they look.
A workable plan

Until you have studied ranges in detail, a simple scheme serves well. From early seats, play big pairs, ace king and ace queen. From the middle, add medium pairs and suited big cards. From the cutoff and button, add small pairs, suited connectors and suited aces. Enter the pot with a raise when you are first in. Fold the rest without regret. This plan is not optimal, but it avoids the common disasters, and it puts you ahead of most casual tables.
The constellation

The Global Positioning System is a fleet of around thirty satellites operated by the United States, orbiting about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. Each completes two orbits a day. They are spread across six orbital planes so that from almost any point on the ground, at least four are above the horizon at once. Every satellite carries several atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts a radio signal that says, in effect, who it is, where it is and what time it is.
Distance from time

A receiver works out its distance from each satellite by timing. The signal carries the moment it was sent. The receiver notes the moment it arrived. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so multiplying the delay by that speed gives the distance. A signal from a satellite directly overhead takes about 67 thousandths of a second to arrive. The measurement has to be extremely fine, since an error of one billionth of a second is an error of 30 centimetres.
Where the spheres meet

Knowing your distance from one satellite places you somewhere on an imaginary sphere centred on it. A second satellite gives a second sphere, and the two intersect in a circle. A third narrows it to two points, one of which is usually out in space and can be discarded. In principle three satellites fix your position. In practice a fourth is needed, for a reason that has to do with the clock in your phone.
The fourth satellite

The satellites carry atomic clocks worth a small fortune. Your phone has a cheap quartz clock that may be off by a great deal. Since distance is computed from time, a bad clock would ruin the answer. The solution is elegant. The receiver treats its own clock error as a fourth unknown, alongside its three coordinates, and uses a fourth satellite to solve for all four at once. As a bonus, every GPS receiver becomes a very accurate clock.
Relativity is built in

The system would not work without Einstein. Clocks on the satellites tick slightly slower because of their speed and slightly faster because gravity is weaker at their altitude. The combined effect is a gain of about 38 millionths of a second per day compared with clocks on the ground. That sounds negligible. Left alone, it would add roughly ten kilometres of position error each day. The satellite clocks are deliberately set to run slow by the right amount before launch.
It only listens

A common misunderstanding is that GPS tracks you. The satellites do not know your receiver exists. They broadcast in all directions, like a radio station, and receivers only listen. Your location is computed inside your device. If your position is shared with anyone, that is done by an app sending it over the mobile network or the internet, which is a separate matter entirely from the positioning system itself.
How accurate

In open sky, a phone typically locates itself to within a few metres. Tall buildings degrade this, because signals bounce off walls and arrive late, making the satellite seem further away. Indoors the signals are often too weak to use. Phones compensate by also using nearby mobile masts and wireless networks. Surveyors and farmers use correction services from fixed ground stations to reach accuracies of a few centimetres.
From military to everyday

GPS was built by the American military, with the first satellite launched in 1978 and the full system operating by 1995. After a Korean airliner strayed into Soviet airspace in 1983 and was shot down, the United States announced the system would be available for civilian use. Until May 2000 the public signal was deliberately degraded. Russia, the European Union and China now operate their own constellations, and modern phones combine signals from all of them.
A diode that glows

A light emitting diode is a diode made from materials that release light when current crosses the junction. The colour depends on the material, not on any coating. Red and green LEDs appeared in the 1960s and 70s. An efficient blue one arrived only in the early 1990s, work that earned Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Blue made white light possible, by coating a blue LED with a phosphor that converts part of its output to yellow.
Voltage is set by colour

Each colour has its own forward voltage. Red runs at about 1.8 to 2.2 volts. Yellow and older green are similar. Blue, white and modern bright green need about 3 to 3.3 volts. This is a property of the part, and you cannot change it. It means a 3 volt coin cell lights a red LED easily and a blue one only barely, and that a red and a blue LED wired directly in parallel will not share: the red one takes nearly all the current.
Why it needs a resistor

Once an LED reaches its forward voltage, a tiny further increase in voltage produces a huge increase in current. Connect one straight to a supply and nothing limits that current except the supply itself. The LED overheats and fails in a fraction of a second, sometimes with a pop. A series resistor absorbs the difference between the supply and the forward voltage and so fixes the current. Subtract the LED's voltage from the supply, divide by the current you want, and you have the value.
How much current to give it

A standard indicator LED is rated for 20 milliamps, but modern ones are so efficient that 1 to 5 milliamps is plenty for a status light indoors. Running at a fraction of the rating saves power and extends life. High power LEDs for lighting are a different animal, running at 350 milliamps to several amps. Those need a constant current driver circuit and a heatsink. A resistor would waste too much power and would not hold the current steady as the LED warms up.
Which leg is which

An LED only lights one way round. On a new through-hole part the longer leg is the anode, the positive side. The plastic rim usually has a flat spot beside the cathode, the negative side. Inside the lens, the larger metal piece is generally the cathode. Surface mount LEDs carry a green mark or a notch at the cathode end. Connecting an ordinary LED backwards at low voltage does not hurt it. It simply stays dark, which makes reversed polarity the first thing to check.
Dimming without changing colour

Lowering the current dims an LED, but the colour of white LEDs shifts slightly as it drops. The preferred method is to switch the LED fully on and fully off very fast and vary the fraction of time it is on. Above a few hundred times a second the eye sees a steady, dimmer light. The technique is called pulse width modulation. Poorly designed dimmers switch too slowly, which is the flicker some people notice in cheap bulbs and car tail lights when their eyes move.
What actually kills them

LEDs do not burn out like filaments. They fade, and heat is the cause. An LED's rated life, often 25,000 hours or more, is the time until its output falls to 70 percent, assuming it is kept cool. In a household bulb the LEDs themselves usually outlast the cramped, hot driver electronics packed in the base. That is why a bulb in an enclosed fixture fails early, and why the first sign of death is often flickering instead of darkness.
Start with the serving size

Every number on a nutrition label refers to one serving, and the serving is stated at the top. It is frequently smaller than what people actually eat. A bottle of drink may contain two and a half servings. A packet of crisps that looks like one portion may be listed as three. Before reading anything else, check the serving size and the number of servings in the pack, and multiply if you plan to eat more.
Calories in context

The calorie figure is the energy in one serving. On American labels, the percentages down the right-hand side are based on a daily intake of 2,000 calories, a round reference figure and not a personal recommendation. Your own needs depend on size, age and activity. The figure is most useful for comparison. Two similar-looking granola bars can differ by a factor of two, and the label is the only way to tell.
The five and twenty rule

The percent daily value column lets you judge quickly whether a food is high or low in a nutrient. As a rule of thumb used by the Food and Drug Administration, 5 percent or less per serving is low, and 20 percent or more is high. For things most people should limit, such as saturated fat, sodium and added sugars, look for low numbers. For things most people lack, such as fibre, calcium and potassium, look for high ones.
Added sugars

Current American labels separate added sugars from the sugars naturally present in milk and fruit. Dietary guidelines advise keeping added sugars below 10 percent of daily calories, which is about 50 grams on a 2,000 calorie diet. A single can of a sugary soft drink contains close to 40 grams. Flavoured yoghurts, breakfast cereals, sauces and breads often contain more than their taste suggests, which is why this line is worth a look.
Sodium

Most of the salt in a typical diet comes from packaged and restaurant food, not from the salt shaker. The general guidance for adults is to stay below about 2,300 milligrams of sodium a day. Soups, cured meats, sauces, bread and ready meals are the usual sources, and a single serving of some can supply half the daily figure. Comparing brands of the same product often reveals large differences, with no difference in taste that most people would notice.
The ingredients list

Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight. The first three make up most of the product. If sugar or a refined flour appears among them, that is what you are mainly eating. Sugar also travels under many names: corn syrup, dextrose, maltose, cane juice, fruit concentrate, honey. A manufacturer can use several kinds so that none appears first. A short list of recognizable ingredients is generally, though not always, a good sign.
Claims on the front

The front of the packet is marketing. The back is regulated information. Phrases such as natural, wholesome or made with real fruit have loose meanings or none. Even regulated terms can mislead. A product labelled reduced fat needs only to have less fat than the original version, and may have more sugar. One labelled multigrain may be mostly refined flour. When the front and the back seem to disagree, believe the back.
A sixty-second routine

For any unfamiliar product: check the serving size, glance at calories, then read three lines, added sugars, sodium and fibre. Scan the first three ingredients. Compare with the product next to it on the shelf. That is enough for nearly every decision. Label formats differ between countries, and some use colour-coded panels on the front, but the same handful of numbers carries most of the information wherever you shop.
A positive test

A disease affects 1 percent of people. A test detects it 90 percent of the time when it is present, and gives a false alarm 9 percent of the time when it is not. You test positive. What is the chance you have the disease? Most people, including many doctors in published studies, answer somewhere near 90 percent. The correct answer is about 9 percent. The error comes from ignoring how rare the disease was to begin with.
Count people, not percentages

The answer becomes obvious if you imagine 1,000 people. Ten have the disease, and nine of those test positive. Of the 990 who are healthy, 9 percent test positive anyway, which is about 89 people. So 98 people have a positive result, and only 9 of them are ill. That is roughly one in eleven. The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer has shown that presenting risks as counts of people in this way sharply improves the accuracy of patients and physicians alike.
What a base rate is

The base rate is the underlying frequency of something in the relevant population: 1 percent in the example. Specific evidence, such as a test result or a description, should adjust that starting figure. It should not replace it. People tend to do the opposite. Faced with vivid, particular information about a case, they forget the background frequency entirely. Psychologists call this base rate neglect, and it appears in medicine, law, hiring and investing.
The stereotype trap

In a classic experiment, people read a description of a man who is shy, tidy and fond of detail, and were asked whether he is more likely to be a librarian or a farmer. Most said librarian, because he fits the picture. They ignored the fact that farmers vastly outnumber male librarians. Even if the description fits librarians several times better, there are so many more farmers that he is still more likely to be one of them.
The inside view and the outside view

Daniel Kahneman described two ways to forecast. The inside view looks at the specifics of your own case: your plan, your abilities, your circumstances. The outside view asks how similar projects have turned out for other people. He told of a team writing a school textbook who estimated two more years of work. Asked about comparable teams, one member admitted that most took seven to ten years and many never finished. Theirs took eight.
Why plans run late

That story illustrates the planning fallacy. People building a schedule imagine the work going according to plan and add a small allowance. They do not consider the many unrelated ways things can go wrong, because no single one is likely. Collectively they are nearly certain. Large construction and software projects overrun as a rule. The reliable correction is to find out how long similar projects actually took and start from that figure, however special yours feels.
Finding the reference class

Using base rates requires choosing a comparison group. For a new restaurant, it might be all restaurants opened in your city in recent years and the share that survived. For a job applicant, the track record of past hires with similar backgrounds. For a home renovation, what contractors' projects of that size typically cost in the end. The class will never match perfectly. An imperfect outside view still tends to beat a detailed inside view built on optimism.
A two-step habit

The practical method has two steps. First, establish the base rate: for things like this, what usually happens? Write the number down. Second, adjust for the particulars of this case, and adjust less than you feel inclined to. If you believe your case is an exception, list the specific reasons and ask whether the people who failed believed the same about theirs. Most of them did. Being special is the most common thing in the world.
The equation

Every balance sheet obeys one rule: assets equal liabilities plus equity. Assets are what the company owns or controls. Liabilities are what it owes to others. Equity is what is left for the owners. The two sides must be equal because everything the company has was paid for with either borrowed money or the owners' money. If the numbers do not balance, an error has been made somewhere, which is the origin of the name.
A snapshot

Unlike the income statement, which covers a period, the balance sheet describes a single moment, usually the last day of a quarter or year. It can look quite different a week later. A retailer's balance sheet just before the holidays, heavy with stock bought on credit, differs from the one in January after the stock has been sold and the suppliers paid. Always note the date at the top before drawing conclusions.
Assets

Assets are listed roughly in order of how quickly they can be turned into cash. Current assets come first: cash itself, money owed by customers, called receivables, and inventory. These are expected to convert to cash within a year. Then come long-term assets: buildings, machinery and equipment, shown at cost minus accumulated wear. Finally there are intangible assets such as patents, and goodwill, which arises when one company buys another for more than its recorded value.
Liabilities

Liabilities are ordered the same way. Current liabilities are due within a year: bills from suppliers, wages owed, taxes due and the portion of loans repayable soon. Long-term liabilities include bonds, bank loans and lease obligations stretching further out. A liability is not a sign of trouble in itself. Buying stock from suppliers on 60 days' credit is a liability and also a cheap source of financing. The question is whether the debts fit the company's ability to pay.
Equity

Equity is the residual: assets minus liabilities. It has two main sources. One is money that shareholders put in when shares were issued. The other is retained earnings, the accumulated profits that the company kept instead of paying out. Equity is also called book value. It is rarely close to what the company is worth on the stock market, since the market looks at future profits and the balance sheet records mostly historical costs.
Can it pay its bills

The first test of health is short-term. Compare current assets with current liabilities. If a company has 2 million dollars of current assets and 1 million of current liabilities, the ratio is 2, a comfortable cushion. A ratio below 1 means that bills coming due exceed the resources on hand to pay them. Some businesses, such as supermarkets that collect cash before paying suppliers, run safely below 1. For most, it is a warning.
How much debt

The second test is long-term. Compare total debt with equity. A company funded mostly by debt earns bigger returns for its owners in good times and is far more fragile in bad ones, because interest must be paid whether or not profits arrive. What counts as too much depends on the industry. Utilities with steady income carry heavy debt safely. A technology firm with unpredictable sales carrying the same load would be taking a serious risk.
Reading it with the others

The three financial statements are linked. Net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet. The change in the cash line between two balance sheets is explained, item by item, by the cash flow statement. Read alone, the balance sheet shows strength at a moment. Read alongside the others across several years, it shows whether that strength is being built up or drawn down, which is the question that matters.
What a limp is

To limp is to enter the pot before the flop by calling the big blind, not raising. Players do it because it costs little and lets them see a flop with a hand they like but do not love. It is the most common play at casual tables and nearly absent from strong ones. When the first player into the pot has a hand worth playing, the better play is almost always a raise. When the hand is not worth a raise, it is usually not worth playing.
A raise can win now

The first argument is simple. A limp cannot win the pot before the flop. A raise can. Every time everyone folds, the raiser collects the blinds without seeing a card. Those small pots add up to a real share of a winning player's profit. A limper gives up that entire source of income and must always make the best hand, or bluff later at greater expense, to win anything at all.
Initiative

The player who made the last aggressive action before the flop holds what is called the initiative. Opponents tend to check to that player on the flop, and a bet from them is believable, because raising before the flop represents a strong hand. This lets the raiser win many pots with a single follow-up bet when nobody has connected. A limper has shown no strength, so a later bet tells a weaker story, and opponents call it more freely.
Fewer opponents, clearer hands

A raise thins the field. Against one opponent, a pair of kings wins about four times in five against a random hand. Against four opponents holding random hands, it wins only about half the time. Limping invites a crowd, and in a crowd even good hands shrink, because somebody usually makes two pair or better. A raise also narrows what the callers can hold, since most players continue against a raise with only their better hands. That makes the rest of the hand easier to read.
Limps invite attacks

At a table with observant players, a limp is a target. It announces a hand that is good enough to play but not good enough to raise. Players behind can raise with a wide range, knowing the limper will usually fold or call and then play out of position with a marginal hand. Over time, limpers pay the blind repeatedly and surrender it repeatedly. A limp is too weak to defend and too expensive to keep abandoning. Watch any table for an hour and note who limps most often. It is rarely the player with the biggest stack at the end of the night.
How much to raise

A standard opening raise is between two and a half and three times the big blind. In live games where players call more loosely, slightly larger is common. If players have already limped in front of you, add about one big blind for each of them. Keep your raise size the same whether you hold aces or a speculative hand. Varying your bet with the strength of your cards gives attentive opponents a free read on your hand.
The exceptions

There are narrow cases where limping is defensible. In the small blind, with only the big blind left to act, a mixed approach of calls and raises is sound. In very passive games where nobody ever raises, limping behind other limpers with a small pair or suited connector can be profitable, because you are getting a good price in a multi-player pot. These are exceptions for specific situations. As a default, the rule holds: if you are the first to enter the pot, raise or fold.
The idea

The Big Bang theory says that the universe was once extremely hot and dense and has been expanding and cooling ever since. It is not a description of an explosion into empty space. Space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies apart, and there is no centre and no edge to the expansion. Run the film backwards and everything we can observe was once packed into a far smaller, hotter region. The evidence for this picture accumulated across the twentieth century.
Galaxies are receding

In the 1920s astronomers found that the light from distant galaxies is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum, a sign that they are moving away. In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître had already proposed, two years earlier, that the universe is expanding, and he argued that it must have begun from a compact initial state he called the primeval atom.
A rival theory

Not everyone accepted this. In the 1940s the British astronomer Fred Hoyle and others proposed that the universe had always existed and always looked much the same, with new matter appearing to fill the gaps as it expanded. It was Hoyle who, on a radio programme in 1949, coined the phrase big bang to describe the idea he opposed. The two theories made different predictions, and for some years there was no observation that could settle the matter.
The afterglow

If the universe began hot, the radiation from that era should still be around, cooled by expansion to a faint glow of microwaves. Physicists predicted this in 1948. In 1964 two radio astronomers at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, found a persistent hiss in their antenna that came from every direction in the sky. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings in case that was the cause. It was the afterglow, and it won them a Nobel Prize.
What the afterglow shows

This cosmic microwave background has since been mapped in great detail by satellites. Its temperature is about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero, nearly identical in every direction, with tiny variations of a few parts in a hundred thousand. Those faint ripples are the seeds from which galaxies later grew. The steady-state theory had no natural way to produce such radiation, and after 1965 it lost nearly all of its support.
The lightest elements

The third line of evidence is chemical. In the first few minutes, the universe was hot enough for nuclear fusion. Calculations predict that this period should have turned about a quarter of the ordinary matter, by mass, into helium, leaving nearly all the rest as hydrogen, with traces of a few other light elements. When astronomers measure the composition of the oldest gas clouds and stars, they find those proportions. Stars alone could not have made so much helium.
The age

Combining the measured expansion rate with the detailed pattern in the microwave background gives an age for the universe of about 13.8 billion years. The oldest stars that have been dated come out slightly younger than that, as they must. The figure is not a guess. It is derived from several kinds of measurement that agree to within a few percent, though a stubborn small disagreement between methods of measuring the expansion rate is an active research problem.
What is still unknown

The theory describes how the universe evolved from a hot dense state. It does not say what, if anything, came before, or why the expansion began. At the very earliest moment the known laws of physics break down. The nature of the dark matter and dark energy that dominate the universe's contents is also unknown. The Big Bang is a well-tested account of the history of the universe from a fraction of a second onward, and it is silent about the instant of origin.
Three legs, one job

A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. A small current flowing into the base allows a much larger current to flow from collector to emitter. With no base current, the path is closed. The ratio between the two currents is the gain, typically 100 or more for a small transistor. So a microcontroller pin that can supply only a few milliamps can, through a transistor, control a motor, a relay or a strip of lights drawing a hundred times as much.
NPN and PNP

Transistors come in two polarities. An NPN transistor turns on when its base is driven positive relative to its emitter and is used to switch the ground side of a load. A PNP transistor is the mirror image, turning on when its base is pulled below its emitter, and switches the positive side. Beginners should start with NPN, since it matches the way logic outputs work: pin high, load on. The common 2N3904 and its cousin the 2N2222 are NPN parts that have been in production for more than half a century.
The standard switch circuit

Connect the load between the positive supply and the collector. Connect the emitter to ground. Connect the control pin to the base through a resistor. When the pin goes high, current flows through the resistor into the base, the transistor conducts and the load turns on. The resistor is essential. The base behaves like a diode to ground, and without a resistor the pin would try to supply unlimited current into it. A value of 1 kilohm suits most small loads driven from 5 volts.
Saturation: fully on

For switching, you want the transistor fully on, a state called saturation, where the voltage left across it is only about 0.2 volts. To guarantee that, supply noticeably more base current than the gain calculation strictly requires. A common rule is to assume a gain of only 10 or 20. For a 100 milliamp load, that means 5 to 10 milliamps into the base. A transistor that is only partly on drops several volts while carrying current, so it runs hot and may fail.
Protecting it from the load

Loads with coils, such as relays, motors and solenoids, kick back with a high voltage spike when switched off. Place a diode across the load with its stripe toward the positive supply and the spike circulates harmlessly. Leave it out and the transistor may work for days before failing, which makes the fault hard to connect to its cause. This diode is the most often forgotten part in beginner circuits, and adding it costs a couple of cents.
When to use something else

A small bipolar transistor is right for loads up to a few hundred milliamps. Beyond that, the base current needed becomes awkward and the 0.2 volt drop starts to waste real power. The usual step up is a MOSFET, which is controlled by voltage and wastes far less at high current. For switching mains voltage or providing complete electrical isolation, use a relay or a solid state relay, with the transistor driving the relay's coil.
Billions of the same idea

The switch you can hold between two fingers is the same idea, in different form, as the ones in a processor. The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947 and was about the size of a thumb. A modern phone chip contains well over ten billion, each a switch turning the next one on or off. Logic gates, memory cells and arithmetic units are all arrangements of switches. Understand one transistor switching one LED and you hold the bottom rung of the ladder that leads to every computer.
Detergents lift grease

Water alone cannot remove oily dirt, because oil and water do not mix. Soaps and detergents solve this with molecules that have one end attracted to water and the other to oil. They surround a particle of grease and allow it to be rinsed away. Washing-up liquid is the most versatile cleaner in the house for exactly this reason. Diluted in warm water, it handles most everyday dirt on most surfaces.
Acids dissolve minerals

The white crust in a kettle, the film on a shower door and the ring in a toilet bowl are mineral deposits left by hard water. They are alkaline and dissolve in acid. Vinegar and citric acid are the mild household options. Commercial descalers and many toilet cleaners use stronger acids. Acids should be kept off marble, limestone and unsealed grout, which are made of the same kind of mineral and will be etched.
Alkalis break down fats

At the other end of the scale, alkaline cleaners attack fats, oils and burnt-on food by turning them into soap-like substances that wash away. Baking soda is the mildest and doubles as a gentle abrasive. Washing soda is stronger. Oven cleaners and drain openers contain lye, which is powerful enough to burn skin and eyes. With anything stronger than baking soda, wear gloves, and with oven cleaner or drain opener, wear eye protection too.
Bleach disinfects

Household bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite. It kills bacteria, viruses and mould and removes stains by destroying coloured molecules. It is not a cleaner in the sense of lifting dirt, and dirt uses up its strength, so clean a surface first and then disinfect it. Disinfectants also need time to work. The label gives a contact time, often several minutes, during which the surface must stay wet.
Never mix bleach and ammonia

Bleach combined with ammonia produces chloramine gases, which damage the lungs. Ammonia is found in some glass and multi-surface cleaners, and in urine, which is why cleaning a cat litter tray or a toilet with strong bleach in a closed room can cause trouble. Exposure brings coughing, burning eyes and shortness of breath. If this happens, leave the area for fresh air at once. Serious breathing difficulty is an emergency.
Never mix bleach and acid

Bleach combined with an acid releases chlorine gas, used as a weapon in the First World War. The acid can be vinegar, a descaler, some toilet bowl cleaners or a rust remover. People do this by accident when one product fails and they pour in another. The safe rule is to never mix bleach with anything except water, and to rinse a surface thoroughly before switching from one product to another.
Other bad combinations

Two different drain cleaners should never be used one after the other, since one may be a strong acid and the other a strong alkali, and they can react violently. Hydrogen peroxide and vinegar combined in one container form a corrosive acid. In general, mixing cleaning products does not make a stronger cleaner. It makes an unpredictable one. Keep products in their original containers with their labels, out of reach of children.
A small sensible kit

Four or five products cover a household. Washing-up liquid for general cleaning. An acid such as white vinegar or citric acid for scale. Baking soda for scrubbing and odours. A disinfectant for the places that need one, such as toilets and surfaces that have held raw meat. Add microfibre cloths and ventilation. Most of the specialized bottles in the cleaning aisle are one of these four types with fragrance, colouring and a higher price.
Planning is biased toward hope

When a team commits to a plan, the mood turns against doubt. People who have reservations keep quiet, because raising problems feels disloyal or negative once the decision is made. The plan is examined mainly by those who wrote it, who see how it is meant to work. Overconfidence builds. Afterwards, when things have gone wrong, everyone can list the causes, and many will say they saw it coming. The knowledge was in the room and never spoken.
The method

The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a simple remedy and called it a pre-mortem. Before the project starts, gather the people involved. Ask them to imagine that it is a year from now and the project has failed badly. Not might fail: has failed. Then give everyone a few minutes, working alone and in silence, to write down every reason they can think of for the failure. Finally, go round the room collecting one reason from each person until the lists are exhausted.
Why imagining it done works

The trick lies in the tense. Research on what is called prospective hindsight found that people asked to explain an event as though it had already happened produced noticeably more reasons, and more specific ones, than people asked why it might happen. Certainty frees the imagination. Explaining a fact is easier than speculating about a possibility, and the mind supplies concrete causes: the supplier who was late, the key person who left.
It makes dissent safe

The second benefit is social. In an ordinary meeting, pointing out a weakness means criticizing a colleague's plan. In a pre-mortem, finding weaknesses is the assigned task, and the person with the most alarming scenario is being the most helpful. Junior people and quiet people, who often see operational problems the leaders do not, are given a turn. Writing alone first matters. It prevents the group from converging on the first idea spoken by the most senior person.
What to do with the list

A long list of ways to fail is only useful if it changes something. Group the reasons and pick the handful that are both likely and damaging. For each, ask three questions. Can we prevent it? Can we detect it early? What will we do if it happens anyway? Some risks lead to a change of plan. Some get an owner and a warning sign to watch. A few are accepted knowingly, which is very different from being surprised by them.
Use it on personal decisions

The exercise works for one person as well as for a team. Before taking a job, moving city or making a large purchase, picture yourself a year on, regretting it. Write the story of what went wrong. The reasons that come easily are the ones to investigate before you commit. Often they point to a question you have been avoiding asking, such as why the last person left the role, or what the commute is really like in winter.
The opposite exercise

A useful companion is to imagine that the project succeeded beyond expectations and to explain why. This reveals what the plan truly depends on: the two or three things that must go right. Sometimes the two lists together show that success rests on a single assumption nobody has tested. That is worth discovering in a meeting room. It is much cheaper than discovering it eight months and most of the budget later.
Keep it short and regular

A pre-mortem need not be elaborate. Thirty minutes at the start of a project is enough, and ten will do for a smaller decision. It can be repeated at major milestones, when circumstances have changed and new failure modes have appeared. The aim is not to talk yourself out of acting. Most plans survive the exercise, modified and with a few risks now being watched. The aim is to act with your eyes open.
Two different measurements

Profit is revenue minus expenses, measured by accounting rules that record a sale when it is earned and a cost when it is incurred. Cash is the money actually in the bank. The two can diverge widely and for long periods. A company can report a healthy profit and be weeks from being unable to pay its staff. Another can report losses for years while its bank balance grows. Understanding why is essential for anyone who runs or invests in a business.
Sales that have not been collected

The first gap is timing of payment. A firm delivers 100,000 dollars of goods in March and sends an invoice due in 60 days. The sale counts as revenue in March. The cash arrives in May, if the customer pays on time. Meanwhile the firm has already paid for materials and wages. On paper, March was profitable. In the bank, March was a large outflow. Money owed by customers is called accounts receivable.
Stock on the shelf

Inventory creates the second gap. Goods bought or made but not yet sold have cost cash, yet they do not appear as an expense until the sale happens. A shop that spends 50,000 dollars stocking up for the season has 50,000 less in the bank and no effect on profit. If the goods sell slowly, cash stays trapped on the shelves. Businesses that fail often have warehouses full of things nobody wanted in time.
Depreciation

The third gap runs the other way. When a company buys a machine for 100,000 dollars that will last ten years, accounting spreads the cost, charging perhaps 10,000 a year as depreciation. The cash went out in full on the day of purchase. In later years, profit is reduced by a depreciation charge that involves no cash at all. This is why a company with heavy equipment can show modest profits while generating plenty of cash, at least until the machines need replacing.
Growth eats cash

Put the first two gaps together and you reach a counterintuitive result: fast growth can kill a profitable company. Each new order requires materials and labour to be paid for now, while the customer pays later. The faster sales grow, the more cash is tied up in receivables and inventory. A firm doubling its sales every year may need outside funding precisely because it is succeeding. Many founders discover this at the worst possible moment.
The cash flow statement

Accountants reconcile the two measures in a third financial statement. It has three sections. Cash from operations starts with net income and adjusts for the gaps described above. Cash from investing records spending on equipment and acquisitions. Cash from financing records borrowing, repayments, share issues and dividends. The three together explain exactly why the bank balance changed over the period. Experienced analysts often read this statement before the others.
Free cash flow

One figure derived from it gets special attention. Free cash flow is cash from operations minus the spending on equipment needed to keep the business running. It is the money genuinely available to repay debt, pay dividends or expand. Because it is harder to flatter with accounting choices than net income is, many investors treat it as the truest measure of what a business produces. A company whose profits consistently exceed its free cash flow deserves a closer look.
For a small business

The lesson for anyone running a small firm is to watch the bank balance as closely as the profit. Forecast cash week by week for the next three months. Invoice promptly and chase late payers. Negotiate longer terms with suppliers and shorter ones with customers. Keep a reserve or a line of credit arranged before you need it. A profitable order that would leave you unable to make payroll in the meantime is an order to restructure or refuse.
Why it is called a 3-bet

The big blind counts as the first bet. An opening raise is the second. A reraise over that is therefore the third bet, or 3-bet. A further raise is a 4-bet. Decades ago, players reraised before the flop only with aces and kings, and everyone knew it. Modern players 3-bet a much wider set of hands, some for value and some as bluffs. Learning to do it, and to respond to it, is one of the clearest dividing lines between beginners and experienced players.
For value

The obvious reason to 3-bet is that you hold a hand that beats most of what the raiser has. With aces, kings, queens and ace king, you want more money in the pot while you are ahead.
